name: Cameroon
summary_text: Article 347-1 of the penal code in Cameroon criminalises both male and female same-sex sexual activity and carries up to five years' imprisonment. The first penal code enacted in 1965 did not criminalise consensual same-sex acts. An ordinance issued in September 1972 by President Ahmadou Ahidjo introduced Article 347bis, now numbered 347-1. The 2016 penal code explicitly outlawed same-sex relations. Under the earlier provision sentences ran between six months and five years.  In Douala on 8 February 2021, two transgender women, Shakiro and Patricia, were arrested in a restaurant for wearing women's clothing. Shakiro, born 29 July 1997 in Douala, had built a Facebook and YouTube following discussing trans life. Both women were convicted of attempted homosexuality, public indecency and failing to carry identification. Each received five years' imprisonment plus a fine of 200,000 CFA francs ($370), the maximum statutory term. They had been detained since February 2021 and spent five months in prison before a judge ordered release pending appeal. An appeal was filed. Defence lawyers Alice Nkom and Richard Tamfu described the verdict as a political decision with no proof of acts. Shakiro subsequently fled Cameroon to claim asylum abroad.  Gender presentation alone has supported convictions in earlier cases. In November 2011 Jonas Kimie and Franky Ndome were sentenced to five years after arrest outside a nightclub. The trial judge treated manner of speech, wearing women's clothing and ordering a cream-based liquor as sufficient evidence of homosexuality. No sexual act was observed. An appeals court acquitted both men on 9 January 2013.  Enforcement extends beyond presentation cases. In 2011 at least a dozen men were detained under Section 347. Jean-Claude Roger Mbede was sentenced to three years at Kondengui Central Prison for sending SMS messages to a male acquaintance. On 24 November 2011 three young men were sentenced to five years for oral sex in a parked car. In May 2005 eleven men were arrested at a nightclub on suspicion of sodomy. Authorities threatened medical examinations to prove activity. The men remained detained into February 2006, with trials scheduled for March 2006 and release in April 2006.  Human Rights Watch documented an uptick of violence in 2022. Since 9 March of that year security forces arbitrarily arrested at least six people and detained eleven people, all victims of group attacks, for alleged consensual same-sex conduct and gender nonconformity. Gendarmes beat two detainees. The organisation found that the criminalisation law enables abuse by civilians and security forces without consequence, a finding attributed to senior researcher Ilaria Allegrozzi. Beatings of gay and trans people in public are reported as common.  Law No. 2010/012 of 21 December 2010 on Cybersecurity and Cybercrime further punishes same-sex propositioning online. Article 83(1) punishes sexual propositions to a person of the same sex through electronic communications with one to two years' imprisonment and a fine of 500,000 to 1,000,000 CFA francs, or one of those penalties. Article 83(2) doubles the penalty where intercourse followed.  Failure to carry identification was charged alongside the anti-homosexuality counts against Shakiro and Patricia. Prison conditions pose an additional risk. Prisoners accused of homosexuality describe the main prison in Douala as hell.

name: Republic of the Congo
summary_text: The Republic of the Congo does not criminalise consensual same-sex conduct between adults. A systematic legislative review in the EUAA May 2024 Query Response Q29 reached that finding, and the United States Department of State human rights reports for 2022 and 2023 record the same position. Same-sex relationships have been legal since 1940.  Penal Code Article 331, as amended in 2006, imposes an unequal age of consent of 21 years for same-sex acts compared with 18 years for different-sex acts. It punishes shameless acts or acts against nature with a person of the same sex under 21 with six months to three years imprisonment and a fine. The EUAA review and the Department of State reports describe the scope of that provision as applied to same-sex conduct as ambiguous, with sources treating it as a basis to justify discrimination.  The provision has not been used for formal prosecution in the reporting period. The 2022 Department of State report states it was not invoked for prosecutions. The 2023 report records no known arrests or prosecutions of LGBTQI+ persons under it during 2023.  Police use the provision in street-level encounters to obtain money. The 2022 report states police at times cited it to extract bribes from gay men. The 2023 report states police continued to use the act against nature law as a pretext to solicit bribes from men. A separate account states police have solicited bribes from young men perceived as gay and have falsely claimed that same-sex activity is generally illegal for that purpose. Such abuses are rarely reported because of fear of police contact, but are investigated when reported.  Local nongovernmental organizations reported violence, psychological and physical harassment, and financial extortion of LGBTQI+ persons by government actors and nonstate actors. The 2023 report describes that pattern as continuing.  The law provides no anti-discrimination protection on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity. There are no hate-crime provisions. There are no provisions addressing discrimination in education, healthcare, housing or employment.  There is no legally recognized procedure to change gender identity.  Same-sex marriage is explicitly excluded. Section 2, Article 127 of the Family Code defines marriage as a public act establishing a lasting union between a man and a woman.  Societal hostility is high. In a survey conducted from 2021 to 2023, 73 percent of people in Brazzaville said they would dislike or strongly dislike having a homosexual neighbour. State authorities and ordinary citizens committed violence against LGBTQ+ people in 2022 and 2023. Reported violence against LGBTQ people is punished by law enforcement.  LGBTQ civil society organizations were present in 2023 but had been unable to obtain legal recognition. In 2020 one nongovernmental organization was denied registration until references to its focus on the LGBTQ+ community were removed.
